title: Distributed-system and message-passing models
summary: Model independent processes, private memory, message passing, events, and the event-history notation used by the lecture.
objectives: Represent process histories and the global event set

sections.title: Independent entities, cooperative work
sections.body: A distributed system is a collection of independent entities that cooperate to solve a problem. In the lecture's model, processes do not share a common global memory and communicate solely by passing messages.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The model is the assumption boundary: if shared memory or reliable global time is silently introduced, later ordering claims become invalid.

sections.title: Events and histories
sections.body: Each process has a sequence of events, and the global event set is the union of those local histories. This notation makes causal order a relation over events rather than an assumption about wall-clock timestamps.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Almost every ordering proof starts by identifying events and the communication edges between them.

reference.sourceId: L. Lamport, Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System

examples.title: Read the distributed diagram
steps: List each process and its local event order.
Mark every send and matching receive.
Avoid inferring order from vertical alignment across processes.
Use the generated relation rules to prove a cross-process order.
examples.answer: The diagram is a partial-order object; geometry is a visual aid, not a global clock.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which model gives each processor its own memory rather than one shared memory space?
contrastDrills.explanation: A multicomputer has processors with private memory connected by a network; a multiprocessor uses shared memory in the lecture's comparison.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

contrastDrills.prompt: What should you use first to prove that one distributed event precedes another?
choices: Their vertical position on the slide
contrastDrills.explanation: Use local order, send-before-receive, and transitivity. Wall-clock position alone does not prove causality.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

math.explanation: The global event set is the union of each process's local history. This lets us define causal relations over events without assuming a shared memory or global clock.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does the message-passing assumption matter before studying logical clocks?
criticalQuestions.angle: Ask what a process knows directly and what information must cross a message boundary.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A process cannot read another process's state directly, so causal knowledge must be carried by messages and represented explicitly.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What mistake occurs when a diagram's vertical alignment is treated as a causal edge?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate drawing layout from the three rules that generate happens-before.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Vertical alignment is not a relation in the model. Only local order, send-before-receive, and transitivity establish causality.
